newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Palestinians blame each other for impasse.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians blame each other for impasse.

text.p: Israelis and Palestinians blamed each other on Monday for what a U.S. official described as a breakdown in the core issues of their 1993 peace accord.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said Washington's refusal to pressure Israel had doomed U.S. efforts to revive Middle East peace talks stuck since March.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office a year ago vowing a tougher line in peace talks, blamed Arafat for the peace crisis which has sparked outbursts of Arab-Israeli violence.

"If there is no forthcoming position on the part of the Palestinians to keep the agreement, that is to fight terrorism and to follow through on the other conditions,...I think it's very hard to proceed," Netanyahu told reporters in parliament.

Washington's ambassador to Israel was telling the two sides what they already knew when he said on Sunday that Israel's building of Jewish settlements and Palestinian violence had shattered the fragile trust between them.
But Ambassador Martin Indyk's comments appeared to strike a sensitive nerve.
In Gaza, Arafat explained the breakdown by saying: "There is no American pressure to save the peace process."
Palestinians have urged Washington, Israel's closest ally, to press Netanyahu to stop building settlements on West Bank land occupied by Israel since 1967.
Israel's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March plunged peacemaking into the most protracted crisis since the right-wing Netanyahu was elected a year ago.
"The core bargain of Oslo has broken down," said Indyk, referring to the landmark 1993 Israel-PLO agreement negotiated in the Norwegian capital.

"Terrorism on the one side and unilateral acts which have created the impression that the final status issues are being pre-empted on the other have combined to break this trust," he told the Israel-U.S. Chamber of Commerce on Sunday.

The Oslo accord, a broad-brush interim agreement that promised security for Israel and self-rule for Palestinians, was aimed at building confidence between the two sides before they tackled thorny "final status" issues.
At times, it did the opposite.

Suicide bombings by Palestinian Islamists opposed to the accord shook the faith of many Israelis in peace while Netanyahu's settlement building and other measures convinced Palestinians they would not obtain the coveted state they view as Oslo's natural outcome.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross, who has logged hundreds of mediation hours, failed to revive peace talks in a nine-day mission that ended last week.

"Since Netanyahu came to power it seems that there has been a retraction in the American perspective in favour of the Israeli perspective," the general-secretary of the Palestinian Authority, Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, told Reuters.
Arafat, disappointed at Ross's performance, asked U.S. President Bill Clinton in a letter sent on Thursday, to personally get involved in efforts to break the impasse.
